analysis.one_liner: Requires companies holding people's personal data to keep reasonable cybersecurity protections, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was introduced with no cosponsors and sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Every business or organization that collects or keeps personal information — Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, biometric data — would have to maintain reasonable cybersecurity protections. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the requirement as an unfair trade practice, could write minimum standards, and its jurisdiction would cover banks, airlines, and nonprofits it normally cannot touch. Violators could face civil penalties above the usual FTC caps to make violations costly enough to deter them.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose names, Social Security numbers, account numbers, and biometric data sit in company databases. Stronger baseline security would lower the odds of the breaches that lead to identity theft, fraudulent card use, and years of cleanup for ordinary people.

how_it_helps.text: Any entity that acquires, maintains, or uses personal information in commerce must have reasonable cybersecurity protections and practices in effect, with no exceptions for banks, airlines, or nonprofits.

The FTC would enforce violations the same way it enforces unfair or deceptive practices, could promulgate regulations setting minimum standards at least as strong as existing federal safeguards for customer information, and could seek civil penalties above the statutory FTC cap when needed to deter violations.

The covered data includes non-truncated Social Security numbers, financial account numbers with access codes, and name-plus combinations like driver's license numbers, biometric identifiers, or account credentials — the information that fuels identity theft when it leaks.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that hold consumer data — retailers, banks, data brokers, health systems, nonprofits — would bear the cost of meeting a federal security standard and of FTC penalties when they fail. Small businesses and charities would face compliance costs too, and consumers might see some of those costs passed through in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to every sole proprietorship, nonprofit, and charity that touches personal information, so small organizations would face compliance costs without the security staff large companies have.

The core standard — 'reasonable cybersecurity protections and practices' — is undefined in the bill and would take shape only through FTC rulemaking, leaving regulated companies and enforcers to litigate what compliance means.

By explicitly overriding the FTC's usual jurisdictional limits to reach banks, savings and loans, credit unions, common carriers, and air carriers, the bill would layer FTC enforcement on top of existing banking and transportation regulators, raising overlap and duplication concerns those industries legitimately raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is real: data breaches keep producing identity theft, and a federal floor on security practices with real penalties would give companies a reason to invest in defense before, not after, the breach. The costs are compliance burdens spread across every sector, heaviest on small organizations, and the vagueness of 'reasonable' protections would take years of rulemaking to settle. The main design gap is that it sets a duty of care but does not create a private right of action for breach victims, so enforcement depends entirely on the FTC's priorities and resources.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late 2017 with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and died there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on September 28, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action was taken in the committee or on the floor for the remainder of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and organizations holding Americans' personal data are better off: no federal security standard was imposed, no expanded FTC enforcement over banks and carriers was created, and no penalty regime above the FTC's usual caps took effect. Consumers exposed to breaches gained nothing from the 115th Congress on this front.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Sen. John Thune (R-SD)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report — after it was referred on September 28, 2017, and the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No party split is visible: a single Democratic senator introduced it, no senator of either party cosponsored it, and no vote was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Data-intensive companies (retailers, tech platforms, data brokers)
industries.note: These firms would have had to meet a federal security standard for the personal data they hold and could face elevated FTC penalties. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers, since the cost of compliance is the cost of preventing the breaches that hit ordinary people.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and common carriers
industries.note: The bill explicitly strips the FTC's usual jurisdictional limits so these regulated firms could be enforced against under the new standard, adding a second regulator alongside banking and transportation authorities. They had a direct institutional interest in the bill going nowhere.

industries.industry: Nonprofits and small businesses handling personal data
industries.note: They would be covered entities too, facing compliance duties without large security staffs. Consumers benefit from their securing data, but the compliance burden falls hardest here.
